title: Bias terms and decision boundaries
goals: Calculate a weighted score with a bias term
Locate and test a two-feature decision boundary
Explain how changing the bias shifts a boundary without training

prerequisite.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [3, 5], what are the contributions and dot product?
prerequisite.answer: The contributions are 6 and -5, giving dot product 1.

vocabulary: An additive parameter applied after a weighted sum
Input locations where the declared classification rule changes class
A weighted sum plus a constant offset
A stated comparison that converts a score into a class

lesson.title: Add an offset to a weighted score

blocks.text: Use the fictional parcel schema [width in cm, height in cm]. Our model computes z = 2 times width - height - 3. The weights are [2, -1]; the bias b is -3. Compute the weighted sum first, then add the bias once. The result is an affine score: a weighted sum plus a constant offset.

Now declare a classification rule: predict class 1 when z is at least 0, and class 0 when z is below 0. Equality belongs to class 1. These are invented categories for arithmetic practice, not a real parcel decision. The weights and bias are supplied, so this is a forward calculation, not training.
A bias is a mathematical parameter. It is not the same use of the word as unfair treatment; numerical offset alone does not establish whether a system is fair.

Set z to zero to locate the boundary: 2 times width - height - 3 = 0, so height = 2 times width - 3. Plot width on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis. Boundary points include (2, 1), (3, 3) and (4, 5). Join them with a straight line and label the axes in cm.

At width 3, height 2 gives score 1 and class 1; height 3 gives score 0 and class 1; height 4 gives score -1 and class 0. Under this axis convention class 1 lies on or below the boundary. One point on each side checks that orientation.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes valid numerical measurements in the agreed units. Changing >= to > changes the equality case, even though the drawn line remains in the same place.

lesson.title: Track the effect of the bias

blocks.title: Hold the weights fixed while shifting the boundary
blocks.caption: The boundary moves parallel to itself because the weights stay fixed. An increased score does not always change a class: only inputs crossing the declared threshold change.

blocks.label: For [3, 4], compare z and prediction with bias -3 and bias -1. Explain which parameter changed.

lesson.title: Separate a parameter change from evidence

blocks.text: Without a bias, this score would be z = 2 times width - height and its zero line would pass through (0, 0). The offset lets the boundary move away from the origin. In this parcel schema zero dimensions are invalid measurements; the origin is still useful as a point on the extended mathematical graph.

Changing bias from -3 to -1 increases every score by 2, but does not rotate the line. Changing a weight can rotate or otherwise change the boundary. Neither change is automatically an improvement. To compare models, retain labels, a declared metric, the same evaluation records and the separate training, validation and test roles.

The boundary states what this particular formula predicts. It does not establish the true classes of all possible inputs. A point very far from the line need not have a reliable prediction when the model, features or data are inappropriate. The raw score is not calibrated confidence or a physical distance from the line.

blocks.label: A team changes b after seeing final-test mistakes and reports the same cases as an untouched test of the new model. Explain the error and the next step.

blocks.text: Next week, we transform scores with activation functions before discussing layers.

workbook.title: Trace the bias once
workbook.prompt: Use z = 2 times width - height - 3 at [5, 4]. Give the weighted sum, bias, final score and prediction under z >= 0.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weighted sum 10 - 4 = 6; bias -3; score 3; prediction 1. Add the bias once after summing.

workbook.title: Plot and label the boundary
workbook.prompt: For the worked model, find boundary points at width 2 and width 4. Test [4, 4] and [4, 6] to identify the class on each side.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Boundary points (2, 1) and (4, 5). [4, 4] has z = 1 and class 1; [4, 6] has z = -1 and class 0. With height vertical, class 1 is on or below the line.

workbook.title: Check the equality rule
workbook.prompt: At [3, 3], compare prediction under z >= 0 with prediction under z > 0. Does changing this comparison move the zero line?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Score is zero. The >= rule predicts 1; the > rule predicts 0. The zero line remains height = 2 width - 3, but its assigned class changes.

workbook.title: Analyse a new model independently
workbook.prompt: A new model has w = [-1, 2], b = -2, inputs [u, v] and class 1 when z >= 0. Calculate scores and classes for [2, 1], [2, 2], [2, 3]. Write the boundary as v in terms of u. Then change only b to 0 and recompute [2, 1].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores -2, 0, 2 give classes 0, 1, 1. Boundary -u + 2v - 2 = 0 gives v = u/2 + 1. With b = 0, [2, 1] scores 0 and class 1. The score rose 2 and the boundary moved to v = u/2.

workbook.title: Require evidence of improvement
workbook.prompt: A teammate says that raising b must improve the model because all scores rise. What information is needed before accepting an improvement claim?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Higher scores can fix some missed class-1 cases while creating false alarms. Compare with observed labels on the same valid evaluation set under a declared metric, keeping fitting and model choices separate from final testing.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to connect signed arithmetic, linear equations and graph regions. Require the explicit equality policy each time. The classroom formula is hand-selected; it demonstrates prediction and parameter effects, not evidence of successful training.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the dot product in the prerequisite question and review adding a negative constant.
Trace all three table rows. Students circle the one addition of b and identify the equality case.
Complete W1 and derive height = 2 width - 3. Plot the three boundary points on labelled axes.
Use W2 and the guided bias comparison. Check both sides numerically before shading a class region.
Retrieve the rule z >= 0. Run or trace the optional code and compare it with the plotted points.
Complete W3. Distinguish moving the boundary from changing the class assigned at equality; discuss the extended origin.
Collect W4 independently. Check scores, classes, rearranged equation and the effect of changing only b.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Offer the fresh retry after feedback to assess the same ideas with a new boundary.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided [3, 4]: with b = -3, z = -1 and class 0; with b = -1, z = 1 and class 1. Only b changed. Exit: test labels influenced the new bias, so the reused cases are development evidence for the revision. Preserve the original result and evaluate a frozen revision on fresh independent cases.
misconceptions: Compute the dot product, then add one b. Adding b twice implements a different formula.
Correctness also needs target labels. A shifted boundary can trade one error type for another.
This b is an additive parameter. Evaluating unfairness requires context and evidence about outcomes and use.
teacher.assessment: W4 should include all three scores and the equality class, with v = u/2 + 1 before the change. Fresh retry: z = u + v - 5, class 1 if z >= 0. [2, 2], [2, 3], [2, 4] give -1, 0, 1 and classes 0, 1, 1; boundary v = 5 - u. With b changed from -5 to -4, [2, 2] reaches zero and class 1.
teacher.support: Provide graph paper and a partially labelled contribution table. If rearranging equations is difficult, find three zero-score points by substitution first. Extension: multiply all weights and b by positive 2 and explain why scores double while classifications under >= 0 stay the same.
